entries.q: It is not the man who has little, but he who craves more, that is poor.
entries.b: Seneca watched the richest men in Rome live like paupers: anxious, comparing, unable to arrive. His diagnosis was not about money but appetite, which is a budget that never balances no matter how large the income. Look at your own craving ledger today: not just for things, for recognition, novelty, reassurance. A person who needs constant more is poor at any salary. A person who can say this is enough is rich at any of them. The accounting starts with one honest look.
entries.x: Name one craving you fed this week that did not pay. Stop feeding it for a day.

entries.q: He who is not satisfied with a little is satisfied with nothing.
entries.b: Epictetus noticed that dissatisfaction scales: the person dissatisfied with little will be dissatisfied with much, because the mechanism, not the amount, is the problem. The mechanism today is largely a screen: the highlight reels of strangers calibrated daily against your unfiltered mornings. You are not losing the comparison. You are playing a game whose rules were designed for you to lose. Put the machine down for a day and notice what satisfaction feels like without opponents.
entries.x: Take one day off comparison. Notice each urge and let it pass unfed.

entries.q: Remove the opinion of need, and the need is removed.
entries.b: Half of what feels necessary is actually just habitual: the second screen, the bigger car, the packed Sunday. Marcus practiced subtraction as a discipline, testing each possession and obligation with one question: what happens if this goes? Usually nothing, except a strange lightness. You will not sell everything. But everything you are currently carrying deserves one honest weighing, because some of it was picked up by accident and never put down.
entries.x: Remove one possession or obligation today. Notice the actual loss, which is usually nothing.

entries.q: Every possession has a price beyond its purchase: storage, worry, maintenance, attention.
entries.b: The Stoics counted the hidden invoice of ownership. The boat needs the trailer and the trailer needs the driveway and the driveway needs the bigger mortgage. The wardrobe needs the organizing and the organizing needs the weekend. Nothing you own is free after purchase; it all charges rent in attention and worry. Today, price one possession honestly: what does it cost you per month, in money and in mind? The number sometimes argues for selling better than any philosophy does.
entries.x: Price one possession honestly: its full monthly cost in money and attention.

entries.q: True poverty is not the empty purse but the crowded mind.
entries.b: Wealth the Stoics recognized had a strange definition: the unhurried hour, the attention fully given, the day with slack in it. By that measure many busy, well-paid lives are poor, and some simple ones are enormously rich. Your calendar is a form of budget. Look at this week's: how many hours are yours, actually, unclaimed by obligation and noise? Reclaim one. Not to fill it with more doing. To be someone who owns a little of their own time.
entries.x: Reclaim one unhurried hour this week. Defend it like a meeting.

entries.q: Have nothing in your houses that you do not know to be useful, or believe to be beautiful.
entries.b: The Stoic test for keeping a thing is blunt: useful, or truly beautiful, or gone. Everything else is custody without benefit. This applies beyond objects: the commitment that is neither useful nor beautiful, the habit, the subscription, the connection that has become pure maintenance. Run the test on one item today. Most of what fails it has been waiting for permission to leave. Grant it, and feel the shelf get lighter.
entries.x: Run the useful-or-beautiful test on one thing today. Let it go if it fails.

entries.q: Live with the gods, and let simplicity be your ornament.
entries.b: Marcus, who could command any luxury, ate plainly and worked at dawn, and wrote about it as a preference rather than a sacrifice. He had discovered what luxury marketing hides: refinement beyond a point adds clutter, not pleasure. The simple meal eaten with attention beats the elaborate one eaten distracted. Today, do one thing the simple way, deliberately: the walk instead of the scroll, the plain dinner, the unadorned evening. Notice the pleasure that was there all along, under the upgrades.
entries.x: Do one ordinary thing today in the simplest possible way, with full attention.

entries.q: Learn to feel that you have enough, and the feeling is wealth.
entries.b: Enough is not a number; it is a trained perception. Seneca practiced poverty monthly, living on the plainest food and clothes, so that fear of losing everything would lose its grip. The training works in reverse too: the more deliberately you experience enough, the less leverage circumstances have over your peace. Tonight, do a small practice: use what you already have for one need you were about to spend on. The muscle strengthens quietly, and it is the only wealth no market can crash.
entries.x: Meet one need today with what you already have. Feel the muscle work.

entries.q: Ask yourself at every act: is this necessary?
entries.b: Marcus audited his own imperial schedule with this question, which suggests what your calendar deserves. Busyness accumulates by default: the meeting that became standing, the commitment that outlived its purpose, the yes given two years ago by a different person. Necessity is the filter. Some things are necessary for love or duty and must stay. Many are only momentum. Apply the question honestly to one recurring item today, and let the honest answers rearrange the week.
entries.x: Ask of one recurring commitment: is this necessary? Act on the answer.

entries.q: Nothing is enough for the man to whom enough is too little.
entries.b: The treadmill works like this: the upgrade arrives, delivers a short hit of satisfaction, then resets the baseline, and the next lack appears. Epictetus diagnosed the flaw centuries before smartphones: satisfaction sourced from acquisition has a half-life measured in days. There is one known exit, which is changing the source rather than the purchase. Satisfaction sourced from attention, craft, and people does not decay. Buy less this season. Source better instead.
entries.x: Skip one planned upgrade today. Redirect the desire toward something that does not decay.

entries.q: Begin at once to live, and count each separate day as a separate life.
entries.b: Seneca's wealth was mornings: used early, spent deliberately, never surrendered by default to noise. There is a version of your day that starts slowly, with light and a thought instead of a feed, and it costs nothing to test. The day's quality is largely set in its first hour, and the first hour is the cheapest one to defend. Try tomorrow morning simply: wake, water, a page, a plan. The simplicity is not deprivation. It is sovereignty.
entries.x: Give tomorrow's first hour to simplicity: no feed, one page, one plan.

entries.q: Withdraw into yourself as far as you can, but associate with those who will make a better man of you.
entries.b: Simplicity extends past objects into inputs. Every source of noise you admit, the feeds, the channels, the group chats, sets up residence in your head and pays no rent. Seneca curated his reading list the way a gardener weeds: ruthlessly, because attention is soil. Today, cancel one input that is neither useful nor beautiful: the app, the account, the argument. The quiet that follows is not emptiness. It is space, which is where your own thoughts get to live.
entries.x: Cancel one noisy input today. Let the space stay empty for a week.

entries.q: We suffer more often in imagination than in reality, especially in imagining what others think.
entries.b: The opinions of others are a possession you cannot actually acquire, yet we exhaust ourselves acquiring them. Their approval is not yours to own: it shifts with their moods, their information, their interests. The Stoics stopped collecting it, and the simplicity of that ledger is worth studying. What remains when you stop furnishing your life with other people's judgments is a smaller, cleaner house: your own values, your own work, your own standard. It is enough. It was always enough.
entries.x: Stop collecting one person's approval today. Own your standard instead.

entries.q: No man is free who is not master of himself, and boredom mastered is freedom won.
entries.b: The modern mind treats boredom as an emergency requiring instant treatment by screen. But boredom is where the mind digests, plans, and heals. The Stoics let their minds be still without anesthesia and found ideas waiting in the stillness. Today, allow one stretch of genuine boredom: the queue without the phone, the commute without the podcast. The first minutes itch. The minutes after them are worth more than the feed ever paid.
entries.x: Be genuinely bored once today. Let the mind work without anesthesia.

entries.q: Possessions should be like the body's members: present when needed, invisible when not.
entries.b: The Stoics kept few things and used them fully. The measure was not asceticism but alignment: each possession earning its place through service. Audit one category today, the closet, the apps, the commitments, and notice the ratio of used to merely kept. Most households are full of the second kind. The first kind teaches a quiet lesson every time you use it: this is enough, and enough is a form of freedom the surplus never delivers.
entries.x: Audit one category today. Move three unused things toward the door.

entries.q: It is not that we have a short time to live, but that we squander it in obligations we never chose.
entries.b: Seneca's deepest complaint about busyness was not the work itself but the unchosenness: lives filled with commitments that nobody consciously decided, accumulated like sediment. The antidote is not laziness. It is choosing: reviewing the obligations, keeping those that serve, releasing those that only accumulated. Look at one sediment layer today, the recurring thing you would never sign up for now, and release it. The time returns to you, which is the whole point.
entries.x: Release one obligation today that you would not choose again.

entries.q: Be careful to leave the drugs of the mind behind: read few books, but well.
entries.b: Seneca read fewer books than we do and digested them better, rereading, arguing, applying. Consumption is not wisdom; a thousand skimmed pages weigh less than one lived-through chapter. This is simplicity applied to the mind: fewer inputs, deeper processing. Choose your next book the way you would choose a dinner companion: for quality of company, not quantity consumed. Then read it slowly, arguing in the margins. One book that changes you outbids fifty that pass through.
entries.x: Reread ten pages of something that once moved you. Read them slowly.

entries.q: The greatest wealth is a poverty of desires.
entries.b: There is a luxury the market cannot sell because it is manufactured internally: wanting less. Each desire shed is a permanent dividend; no invoice follows. The person who needs little cannot be held hostage by raises, markets, or trends, and their yes and no mean something because need does not vote for them. Test the dividend today: want less of one thing, on purpose, and notice the strange wealth the next morning. It compounds faster than money does.
entries.x: Want less of one thing today, on purpose. Bank the dividend.

entries.q: Enjoy the present without anxious dependence on the future; the simple hour is the whole fortune.
entries.b: We habitually mortgage the present for a future acquisition: this year for the promotion, this season for the holiday. Seneca's simplicity was temporal as much as material: be where your feet are, spend today's wealth, which is attention, on today. The simple hour, fully inhabited, is the actual fortune, and it is available regardless of bank balance. One hour of presence today, uncluttered and complete, outranks most of what the future is promising.
entries.x: Buy nothing this hour. Spend full attention on the present one instead.

entries.q: Order your soul each morning as you would a room: sweep, straighten, air out.
entries.b: External simplicity and internal simplicity feed each other. The cluttered desk breeds the cluttered mind and vice versa, which is why the Stoics ordered both with the same ritual. Ten minutes of physical clearing, the surface, the inbox, the room, buys a measurable return in mental room. Do one ten-minute sweep today, physical and digital. The goal is not beauty. It is the feeling of walking into a cleared space where your own thoughts can be heard again.
entries.x: Do one ten-minute clear today: one surface, one inbox, one room.

entries.q: The cheapest pleasures are the most enduring: light, air, a friend's voice, a task done well.
entries.b: List the best hours of your life. Almost none were expensive. The water on a hot day, the conversation that ran past midnight, the meal after real work. The Stoics catalogued these costless pleasures and made them the center of a rich life, because they cannot be inflated, taxed, or lost in a market crash. Today, spend deliberately on the free list: sunlight, movement, one unhurried conversation. The budget is zero, and the return embarrasses the expensive ones.
entries.x: Enjoy three costless pleasures today, deliberately and with attention.

entries.q: Set a limit for yourself which, once reached, you will pass no further.
entries.b: Seneca told Lucilius to fix a limit for wealth and stop there, because a limitless chase has no finish line by definition. The modern version applies to everything: the inbox, the achievements, the followers, the renovations. Draw one line today in some domain: this much money, this size of home, this many commitments, and then. The line is not resignation. It is the moment the rest of life, the part that was waiting, gets funded.
entries.x: Draw one enough-line in some domain of your life. Write it down.

entries.q: Do not seek to have everything that seems good; seek to will only what is truly yours.
entries.b: Much of what we pursue was never our standard: it was absorbed from parents, peers, and feeds, and pursued on autopilot. The career shape, the timeline, the definition of success. Epictetus asked for an audit: which desires are actually mine? Some pass the test and deserve full effort. Many are borrowed, and chasing them spends your one life on someone else's furnishings. Today, reclaim one desire and release one borrowed one. The house gets lighter and truer.
entries.x: Identify one borrowed desire today. Return it, and reclaim one of your own.

entries.q: Practice refusing things, so that one day you can refuse what matters.
entries.b: Musonius trained his students in small refusals: a favorite food skipped, a comfort declined, so that when a real temptation arrived, the refusal muscle had reps. Self-restraint is not a mood; it is a muscle with a training history. Today, take one small restraint rep: the snack skipped, the purchase postponed, the extra episode declined. It costs almost nothing and it strengthens the exact muscle that will hold when the big test comes.
entries.x: Take one small restraint rep today. Skip something you easily could have.

entries.q: Speak simply: let your words be plain, and let them match your deeds.
entries.b: Complication in speech usually hides something: the hedge, the spin, the version of events edited for advantage. Simplicity of speech is therefore an ethical practice, not a style. Say the plain thing: this is what I did, this is what I want, this is what I can and cannot do. It is riskier in the moment and cheaper over a lifetime, because a plain truth needs no maintenance. Say one plain thing today that you would normally wrap in three layers.
entries.x: Say one plain, unlayered truth today. Feel the cost and the saving.

entries.q: Whether you eat or walk or talk, do it with the whole soul; hurry is the enemy of both virtue and digestion.
entries.b: Hurry is simplicity's opposite, and it has colonized even our meals, eaten standing, over screens, between tasks. The Stoic practice was unhurried attention on one thing at a time, and the meal was its daily rehearsal. One meal today, eaten slowly, without a screen, with the food actually tasted: this small ritual retrains the whole day's tempo. The world will not fall apart in twenty unhurried minutes. It never has.
entries.x: Eat one meal today slowly, screenless, with the food actually tasted.

entries.q: Do not fill every hour. The empty ones are where the self is kept.
entries.b: A fully booked calendar feels productive and functions as erasure: the white space is where thinking happens, where feelings catch up, where relationships wander past their agenda. The Stoics kept unscheduled hours deliberately, knowing that the unscheduled is where the actual self survives its obligations. Find one empty hour this week and do not fill it. Let it be strange and slightly boring. That is the feeling of your own mind having room again.
entries.x: Leave one hour this week completely unscheduled. Do not fill it.

entries.q: Wealth is not the having of much, but the wanting of little, rightly ordered.
entries.b: Seneca conducted his wealth audit backwards: not counting assets but counting wants. The second number is the one that determines poverty or riches, and unlike the first, it is directly controllable. Run the audit tonight: what do you want, itemized? Then mark each item: mine already, earnable honestly, or negotiable. The list is almost always shorter than the feeling of lacking suggested, and the shrinking of it is the only wealth that requires no luck.
entries.x: Itemize your wants tonight. Mark each: have, earnable, or unnecessary.

entries.q: Most of what we want we want because others have it.
entries.b: Watch a desire form in real time: someone else acquires, and the want arrives a half-second later, wearing your face but speaking their voice. This is the human default, and unchecked it guarantees a life of chasing moving targets set by strangers. Interrupt one transmission today: when the want arrives, ask whether it existed five minutes ago. If not, it is not yours. Send it back. The wants that survive the check are the ones worth serving.
entries.x: Catch one borrowed want today, check its origin, and decline it.

entries.q: A month of less: look at what you carried out, and how the shoulders feel.
entries.b: A month of subtraction leaves evidence: the canceled things, the released commitments, the quieted inputs. Notice the ledger now. Less noise, fewer wants, more hours that belong to you. This is the Stoic paradox, that reduction is the strangest form of gain, and it compounds monthly for the rest of your life. The practice from here is maintenance: one honest subtraction whenever the weight starts creeping back. The shoulders already know the arithmetic.
entries.x: Name one subtraction from this month that gave back the most.

entries.q: A month of less: count what remains, and find it enough.
entries.b: A month of subtraction leaves its evidence: the canceled inputs, the released obligations, the purchases declined and not missed. Look over the ledger tonight. What remains is both lighter and truer: fewer things, more deliberately chosen; fewer wants, more honestly yours. This is the Stoic paradox, that reduction is the strangest form of gain, and it compounds monthly for a lifetime. The practice from here is maintenance: one honest subtraction whenever the weight starts creeping back.
entries.x: Name one subtraction from this month that gave back the most, and guard it.
